dt4_the_case_law.topic: Campaign-finance case law from Buckley to McCutcheon

claims.text: Buckley v. Valeo, 30 Jan 1976, per curiam: upheld contribution limits, aggregate annual limit, disclosure, voluntary public funding with spending limits; struck candidate expenditure limits, independent expenditure limits and limits on candidates' own funds; spending limits 'necessarily reduce the quantity of expression'; corruption or its appearance justifies contribution limits; independent expenditures found not comparably dangerous; FECA amendments signed by Ford 15 Oct 1974

Citizens United v. FEC, 21 Jan 2010: 5-4 (Kennedy with Roberts, Scalia, Alito, Thomas) struck BCRA s.203 limits on corporate and union independent expenditures; overruled Austin (1990) and part of McConnell (2003); disclosure upheld 8-1 with Thomas alone dissenting on that part; Stevens dissent (Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor): 'A democracy cannot function effectively when its constituent members believe laws are being bought and sold'; case arose from Hillary: The Movie (2008)

SpeechNow.org v. FEC, D.C. Circuit en banc, unanimous, 26 March 2010: contribution caps violate the First Amendment as applied to an independent-expenditure-only group; organizational, recordkeeping and reporting rules upheld; direct-to-candidate limits untouched

McCutcheon v. FEC, 2 April 2014, 5-4: Roberts plurality (Scalia, Kennedy, Alito), Thomas concurring in judgment and would strike all contribution limits; Breyer dissent (Ginsburg, Sotomayor, Kagan); aggregate biennial limits struck (2011-12: $46,200 to candidates, $70,800 to parties, $117,000 combined); base per-candidate limit kept

Arizona Free Enterprise Club v. Bennett, 27 June 2011, 5-4 (Roberts; Kagan dissent with Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor): struck Arizona's matching-funds trigger, which gave publicly financed candidates extra funds when outspent by opponents or independent groups, up to three times the base grant; the scheme 'substantially burdens' speech

dt4_who_spends.topic: Who spends: 2024 and 2026 outside money, every major spender

claims.text: OpenSecrets (to mid-Oct 2024): outside spending on 2024 federal elections a record $4.5bn, more than half from groups that do not fully disclose funding; super PACs reported over $1bn from shell companies and dark-money groups; presidential outside spending over $2bn vs about $1.14bn in 2020; anonymous-source money under $71.7M in 2016, $653M in 2020, $617M in 2022

OpenSecrets 2024 spenders: Future Forward USA PAC about $517.1M ($136.4M from its dark-money arm Future Forward USA Action; Bloomberg $19M to the PAC and a reported $50M to the nonprofit; Moskovitz $38M; Hoffman $10M; Democracy PAC $10M); MAGA Inc. about $377M (Timothy Mellon $151.5M); America PAC over $169M (Musk about $118.6M since summer); Preserve America over $112.2M (about $100M from Miriam Adelson); Right for America about $69.6M (Perlmutters)

OpenSecrets 2024 party-aligned groups: Congressional Leadership Fund nearly $216.7M (American Action Network about $40M); Senate Leadership Fund over $211M (One Nation about $54M); House Majority PAC over $196.1M; Majority Forward over $113.2M in contributions, $70.8M to Senate Majority PAC; WinSenate about $309M; four leadership-aligned nonprofits about $250M from anonymous donors; Ohio Senate race over $308M outside spending

Issue One: Jan 2025-June 2026 the four leadership super PACs (SLF, CLF, SMP, HMP) raised $714.6M, of which $197.7M from affiliated dark-money groups: One Nation to SLF $70.74M, American Action Network to CLF $44.2M, Majority Forward to SMP $61M, House Majority Forward to HMP $21.7M; Republican-aligned 58%, Democratic-aligned 42%

Marketplace 21 Oct 2026: OpenSecrets' McCreary: 'The top six spenders each spent $60 million apiece through Oct. 5', together over a third of total; outside groups 'tend to lean to the right'; Democratic candidates have tended to outraise Republicans; MiQ projects 2026 the most expensive cycle

Fairshake (formed 23 Mar 2023) with affiliates Protect Progress (Democratic primaries) and Defend American Jobs (Republican primaries): donors Coinbase $93.5M, Ripple $45M, Andreessen and Horowitz $33.5M each, Jump $25M; spent over $133M in 2024, nearly twice as much on Republicans; over $10M against Katie Porter; backed winner in 33 of 35 primaries by June 2024; $193M+ raised for 2026 by Jan 2026; 2026: $12M for Barry Moore (AL), $10M against Juliana Stratton (IL)
The 74 (OpenSecrets data, 1 Nov 2024): AFT PAC raised about $12M and spent about $13M in 2024, including $3M to Senate Majority PAC and $1.6M to House Majority PAC

Commonwealth Foundation (advocacy, 8 Dec 2025): NEA, AFT, SEIU and AFSCME spent more than $915M on 'political and ideological causes' in 2023-24, nearly $650M (over 85%) from dues; method not described on the page; scope broader than federal elections

dt4_what_money_buys.topic: What money buys: research, cases and opinion

claims.text: Bonica (2016), 5,005 congressional candidates 2010-14: predicting that the top fundraiser wins is right in 79% of contested primaries vs 58% for a model on candidate characteristics; evidence predictive/descriptive, not causal; lawyers about 54 times more likely to run and 99 times more likely to be elected than the average citizen

Cox (2024 working paper, House 2002-18 structural model): super PACs have 'muted equilibrium effects due to political competition', on average helping Republicans; without them Republican general-election vote share falls about 2.2% (95% CI about -3.0% to +0.2%), about 6-7 seats per cycle; Republican incumbents gain about 3.2% in primaries; super PACs mostly backed challengers; Democratic incumbents about 1.4% more likely to take extreme positions without super PACs

Pew (10-16 July 2023, n=8,480): 72% favour limits on campaign spending by individuals and organisations, 11% no limits, 16% unsure; 80% say donors have too much influence on Congress; 73% say lobbyists and special interests do; 70% say district residents have too little influence; nearly six in ten think effective new laws are possible (Republicans 52%, liberal Democrats 76%)
University of Maryland PPC/Voice of the People (reported 10 May 2018): about three-quarters backed a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, Republicans 66%, Democrats 85%
Bloomberg spent more than $1bn of his own money on the 2020 Democratic primary, suspended 4 March 2020 after Super Tuesday, winning 61 delegates and only American Samoa

Wisconsin Supreme Court, 1 April 2025: Susan Crawford beat Brad Schimel by 10 points; Musk spent more than $20M backing Schimel, about one in five dollars; total over $100M, the most expensive court race in US history
